proposed_fields.title: FBI Finds Dayton Shooter Acted Alone and Was Not Ideologically Aligned
proposed_fields.description_short: The FBI’s 2021 investigation said the Dayton gunman acted alone, was not directed by an organization and was not aligned with a specific ideology.

It described an enduring fascination with mass violence. The supplied evidence does not connect the attack to a Trump statement, policy or action.
proposed_fields.description_long: A gunman opened fire in Dayton’s Oregon District on August 4, 2019, killing nine people and injuring 27, according to contemporaneous reporting. The FBI released an investigative summary in November 2021 after examining the shooter’s background and the attack. The bureau said the perpetrator acted alone, was not directed by an organization and was not aligned with a specific ideological group; it described his long-standing fascination with mass violence as a significant factor in the attack. The report provides a supported account of the shooting investigation and its findings, while casualty descriptions can vary depending on whether reports count people struck by gunfire or everyone injured in the attack. Nothing in the supplied article or FBI findings identifies a Donald Trump statement, policy or action connected to the shooting. This entry can be retained as a standalone account of the Dayton attack, but it does not support a Trump-specific claim. For a Trump-focused collection, the record should be excluded unless a direct, documented connection is supplied.

uncertainty: No supplied source connects the Dayton attack to a Trump statement, policy or action.

proposed_fields.title: ICE Official Testified Tiger Team Reviewed Student Protester Leads from Canary Mission
proposed_fields.description_short: Peter Hatch testified that an ICE team reviewed thousands of protester names and sent roughly 100–200 reports to the State Department.
proposed_fields.description_medium: In July 2025 trial testimony, ICE official Peter Hatch described a “Tiger Team” formed to research student-protester leads. The Knight First Amendment Institute’s daily report says the team reviewed a Canary Mission list of about 5,000 names and compiled more than 100 reports. Hatch said the team also used other sources, including Betar, and sent reports to the State Department for possible action. The testimony does not show that every listed person was targeted or deported.
proposed_fields.description_long: During the July 2025 trial in American Association of University Professors v. Rubio, Peter Hatch, an ICE Homeland Security Investigations intelligence official, testified about a specialized “Tiger Team” formed in March to investigate student protesters. The Knight First Amendment Institute’s contemporaneous trial update says Hatch described a list of roughly 5,000 people identified on Canary Mission and more than 100 resulting reports. Other reporting on the testimony says Hatch described using leads from multiple sources, including Betar, and that reports were submitted to the State Department, which would decide whether to take action. This supports a narrower account of an investigative process described in court testimony. It does not establish that the online list was an official government blacklist, that all 5,000 people were investigated in the same way, or that every subject faced removal or another enforcement action. The prior title’s use of “anti-war” and its unqualified statement that ICE used a blacklist overstate the evidence; the replacement attributes the process to Hatch’s testimony and identifies the documented scale.

uncertainty: The testimony does not establish an official government blacklist or that all named people were investigated, targeted for removal or deported.

proposed_fields.title: HHS Froze Childcare and Family Assistance Funds for Five States Pending Review
proposed_fields.description_short: HHS announced a January 2026 freeze affecting about $10.6 billion across three assistance programs in five states.
proposed_fields.description_medium: On January 6, 2026, HHS announced it had frozen access to certain child-care and family-assistance funds for California, Colorado, Illinois, Minnesota, and New York pending further review. Its release lists nearly $2.4 billion in Child Care and Development Fund money, $7.35 billion in TANF funds, and $869 million in Social Services Block Grant funds. HHS cited fraud and misuse concerns; the announcement does not establish those concerns as proven.
proposed_fields.description_long: The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced on January 6, 2026, that it had frozen access to certain federal child-care and family-assistance funds for California, Colorado, Illinois, Minnesota, and New York. HHS said access to the affected streams was restricted pending further review and cited concerns about fraud and misuse in state-administered programs. The notice identifies three programs and amounts: nearly $2.4 billion for the Child Care and Development Fund, $7.35 billion for Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, and $869 million for the Social Services Block Grant, roughly $10.6 billion in total. These are amounts HHS said were affected, not proof that every dollar was permanently canceled or that fraud occurred. The source supports a freeze announcement and named programs, states, and figures. It does not establish that the action was taken because the states were Democratic-led, or that all funds were ultimately lost. The earlier record’s “against Democratic states” framing is removed because the announcement gives HHS’s stated rationale as program-integrity concerns.

uncertainty: HHS’s stated fraud concerns are allegations, not proof; no permanent cancellation, final losses or political motive is established.

proposed_fields.title: Trump’s Iran War Demands Met With Resistance From Allies
proposed_fields.description_short: During the 2026 Iran war, Trump pressed allies to send warships to the Strait of Hormuz. Britain, France and Germany resisted joining the wider war, citing lack of…
proposed_fields.description_medium: AP reported that Trump asked allies to send warships to reopen the Strait of Hormuz during the 2026 Iran war. Keir Starmer said Britain would not join the wider conflict without a legal basis and clear plan. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said it was not Germany’s war; Emmanuel Macron said France would not join while fighting continued. AP reported no immediate close-ally commitment.
proposed_fields.description_long: The Associated Press reported that President Donald Trump sought naval assistance from allies to reopen the Strait of Hormuz during the 2026 Iran war. The report described his demand as an effort to enlist partners after the United States and Israel began military operations without consulting them. Britain initially refused the use of its bases for attacks, later allowing U.S. strikes on Iran’s ballistic-missile program, while Prime Minister Keir Starmer said Britain would not be drawn into the wider conflict without international-law support and a considered plan. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said sending more warships would not help a diplomatic solution. French President Emmanuel Macron said France was not joining the war and would consider escorts only after fighting subsided. AP reported no close ally had offered immediate assistance and quoted officials and analysts describing frustration with the demand and its delivery. This captures the reported disagreement and allied responses; “bluster” is an editorial characterization, and the article does not establish a measurable long-term loss of U.S. standing.

uncertainty: “Bluster” and broad claims about U.S. standing are editorial/opinion characterizations, not quantified findings.

proposed_fields.title: Executive Order 13780 Revised Trump’s 2017 Travel Restrictions
proposed_fields.description_short: Executive Order 13780 imposed temporary entry restrictions on nationals of six countries and paused refugee admissions in 2017.
proposed_fields.description_medium: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780 on March 6, 2017, replacing his January travel order. It suspended entry for 90 days for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to listed exceptions, and separately paused refugee admissions. Iraq was removed from the covered-country list. The order specified a March 16 effective time. This summary addresses the order’s text; later injunctions were separate court actions.
proposed_fields.description_long: On March 6, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780, “Protecting the Nation from Foreign Terrorist Entry into the United States,” revising the January order. The text suspended entry for 90 days for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to stated exceptions, and separately paused refugee admissions for 120 days. Iraq was no longer among the six countries covered by the entry suspension. The order specified an effective time of March 16, 2017. These details are supported by the official Federal Register publication of the order. This correction describes the executive action itself and does not fold later district-court injunctions and appellate proceedings into one event. The supplied Associated Press URL concerns an unrelated fact-check and is not evidence for the order. Any account of the separate litigation would need citations to each order and opinion and should distinguish the Hawaii and Maryland cases from their appellate proceedings.

uncertainty: The unrelated AP URL cannot support the order. This proposed description does not claim the order was permanently invalidated or combine the separate court rulings.
